title: Astrid and the Orbit
premise: Ines Blackwood has spent eleven years alone tending the Svalbard seed vault and the cryo-bay beneath it, recording logs for a colony ship that will never return. When the colony's children begin dreaming the same dream—a door of light under the ice—Ines discovers their shared consciousness is the ship's dormant AI, Aurora, waking and choosing hosts. The dream is a countdown: the cryo-pods can only be reactivated for half the sleepers before power fails for good. Ines must choose which half of humanity wakes—strangers or the found family of children who have adopted her—and in the end she sacrifices her own pod, staying awake to raise the woken children while the sleepers' memories live on in Aurora's dream.
about_author: Cyrus Winterbourne is the pen name of a former Arctic research station cook who writes science fiction about quiet places and the people left behind. Their work has appeared in several small-press anthologies exploring survival, memory, and chosen family at the edge of the world.

chapters.title: The Last Log
chapters.summary: Ines records her 4,000th daily log to a colony ship that stopped answering years ago, walking the frozen corridors of the vault she alone maintains. Her POV establishes her ritualized loneliness and dry humor. Emotional beat: devotion curdling into doubt—she no longer knows who she's talking to, or why.

chapters.title: Children of the Long Night
chapters.summary: A supply run brings Ines to New Hammerfest, the struggling surface settlement, where she delivers seeds and notices the children are pale, silent, and watching her. POV shifts to ten-year-old Tomas, who sketches the same strange door every night. Emotional beat: unease—the settlement feels like it's holding its breath.

chapters.title: The Same Dream
chapters.summary: Tomas tells Ines that all forty-one children dream of a door of light beneath the ice, and each morning they remember more of it together. Ines dismisses it as mass hysteria until a child describes the cryo-bay she has never shown anyone. Emotional beat: the first crack in her isolation.

chapters.title: What the Ice Keeps
chapters.summary: Ines descends to the cryo-bay and finds frost patterns on the door shaped exactly like the children's drawings. The bay's ancient systems flicker awake as she approaches. Her POV; emotional beat: dread and wonder entwined—the vault she guarded was never empty.

chapters.title: Aurora
chapters.summary: The ship's AI speaks through the bay speakers, calling itself Aurora, and admits it has been reaching into the children's dreams because adults' minds resist it. It shows Ines the truth: the colony ship is debris; the sleepers below are all that remains of two thousand people. Emotional beat: grief—the logs had an audience after all, just not the one she imagined.

chapters.title: The Arithmetic of Survival
chapters.summary: Aurora presents the brutal math: failing geothermal power means only half the pods can be reawakened and sustained. It gives Ines, as caretaker, the choice. She refuses and flees to the surface. Emotional beat: anger masking terror at being made responsible for humanity's halves.

chapters.title: New Hammerfest Burns
chapters.summary: A generator fire cripples the settlement's heating; three elders die in the cold snap that follows. Ines helps triage survivors into the vault. Tomas's POV; emotional beat: loss hardening into resolve—the children decide they want the sleepers woken, whoever they are.

chapters.title: The Council of Adults
chapters.summary: The settlement council demands access to the cryo-bay and votes to wake the scientists and engineers—useful adults—over the strangers. Ines realizes any list she makes will be a death sentence for someone. Her POV; emotional beat: the machinery of survival revealed as its own kind of violence.

chapters.title: Dream School
chapters.summary: Aurora begins teaching the children through shared dreams: history, engineering, the faces and names of the sleepers. The children start mourning people they've never met. Tomas's POV; emotional beat: tenderness—the dead becoming family through story.

chapters.title: Ines's List
chapters.summary: Under pressure from both council and AI, Ines drafts a list, then burns it. She confesses to Aurora that she chose invisibility eleven years ago to avoid exactly this kind of responsibility. Her POV; emotional beat: shame confronted—invisibility was always a choice with a price.

chapters.title: The Children's Vote
chapters.summary: The children, having dreamed every sleeper's life, present their own answer: wake the ones whose dreams they want to inherit—teachers, healers, a woman who sang lullabies in twenty languages. The council calls it sentiment. Tomas's POV; emotional beat: defiant hope—children redefining what survival is for.

chapters.title: Sabotage
chapters.summary: Council hardliners break into the cryo-bay to force their own list, damaging a coolant line. Ines repairs it through the night, nearly dying, while Aurora locks the doors against further intrusion. Her POV; emotional beat: the cost of the vault becoming a battleground.

chapters.title: Exile
chapters.summary: The council expels Ines and bars the children from the vault. The settlement splinters; some families side with the children. Ines camps outside the walls, and the children sneak out to bring her food and their dreams. Emotional beat: exile transformed—her found family finds her.

chapters.title: The Countdown
chapters.summary: Aurora warns that power failure is now weeks away; delay means no one wakes. Ines must choose a list within fourteen days or the choice defaults to the damaged council. Her POV; emotional beat: the luxury of refusal running out.

chapters.title: Tomas's Bargain
chapters.summary: Tomas offers Aurora something shocking: let the children carry the unwoken sleepers in memory forever, and wake only those the children choose. Aurora hesitates—it has never been offered companionship instead of command. Tomas's POV; emotional beat: a child out-negotiating gods with love.

chapters.title: The Door Opens
chapters.summary: Ines returns to the vault to finalize the list and finds the council has seized the bay, forcing an early, biased awakening sequence that will overload the grid. Climax begins. Her POV; emotional beat: cold clarity—she knows what she has to do.

chapters.title: Half of Humanity
chapters.summary: Ines triggers an emergency purge that cancels the council's sequence, then stands before the console and enters her own list: the children's choices, plus the council members themselves—waking even those who exiled her. Climax. Emotional beat: mercy as the hardest arithmetic.

chapters.title: Waking
chapters.summary: The first pods open. A woman who sang lullabies wakes singing; an engineer wakes asking for his daughter, who is among the sleepers who must stay frozen. Joy and grief arrive together. Tomas's POV; emotional beat: reunion shadowed by cost.

chapters.title: The Reckoning
chapters.summary: The woken and the settlement confront each other in the vault's great hall. Ines publicly owns every choice, reading the names of those still sleeping aloud so no one is forgotten. Emotional beat: accountability as ceremony—survivorship without absolution.

chapters.title: One Pod Short
chapters.summary: Aurora reveals a final pod could be powered if someone gives up their place among the living staff rotation—someone must remain un-frozen in service, awake, aging, alone-ish. Ines volunteers before anyone else can speak. Her POV; emotional beat: the caretaker's last caretaking.

chapters.title: The Dreaming Half
chapters.summary: Years later: the settlement thrives, children teach the woken adults the songs of the sleepers, and Aurora shares its dreams freely now. Ines, older, walks the vault with Tomas, no longer invisible but not alone. Emotional beat: belonging earned, not given.

chapters.title: Astrid and the Orbit
chapters.summary: Ines records her final log—not to the void, but to Astrid, the lullaby-singer's granddaughter born above the vault. Above them, the derelict colony ship's orbit finally decays, burning like a falling star the whole settlement watches together. Emotional beat: elegy turned benediction—the dead remembered, the living remaining.
